processes.description: Operations accounting sets the allocation of Texas Operations costs across cost centers, both for the annual plan and month by month. Brenda Herod sends allocation files and asks managers to review them and update the spreadsheet with changes; Lisa Cousino sets up responsibility centers (RCs), announces charges that will or will not appear, and asks staff to check their RC reports for misposted charges. Labor Distribution and budget-versus-actual reports are distributed, and staff flag people or charges showing in the wrong place so they can be corrected.
steps: Accounting prepares the plan or monthly allocation file for Texas Operations.
The allocation is sent to managers, who review it and return changes.
The allocation spreadsheet is updated and the final allocation is issued.
Monthly RC, Labor Distribution and budget-versus-actual reports are distributed.
Staff check their RC and labor reports for misposted charges or employees.
Misposted charges are reported and corrected with the RC owner or corporate.

stalls.summary: Spreadsheet tooling breaks during allocation updates: the person updating the allocation gave up on the spreadsheet after being unable to insert a column.
Corporate IT invoices for months were not billed on time, so RC reports omitted IT charges and owners had to wait for them to appear later.

Requests are unclear or have no obvious owner: a recipient did not understand what was being asked, someone had to ask who handles Labor Distribution reports, and one item 'just sits' because nobody wants to touch it.

automation.approach: Keep the allocation percentages in one shared, structured workbook with a fixed layout per cost center, and generate a monthly exception report that compares RC postings against the allocation and the employee roster, flagging misposted charges and people showing in the wrong RC for owners to confirm.
automation.rationale: Most rework comes from editing ad hoc spreadsheets and from owners eyeballing RC reports for errors. A standard allocation template removes the broken-spreadsheet step and gives reviewers a consistent sheet to mark up, while an exception check narrows manual review to the flagged lines.

work_estimate.rationale: A round means building or revising an allocation file, reviewing it against plan, updating the spreadsheet with managers' changes, or checking an RC or labor report line by line and getting a correction made. Around 45 minutes covers the spreadsheet work and the check; plan allocations and corrections run longer. Template layout and exception flagging could take about half, leaving judgement on percentages and corrections.

processes.description: Written confirmations of gas purchases and sales are executed and passed on. A marketer executes a sales confirm and sends a copy to colleagues, counterparties ask for copies to be faxed or forwarded, and counterparties chase confirmations for months they never received. Senders are not always sure how the confirmation reaches the people who need it.
steps: A gas purchase or sale is agreed with a counterparty.
The confirmation is prepared and executed.
A copy is sent to internal colleagues and to the counterparty.
Missing confirmations are requested by the counterparty and resent.

stalls.summary: A counterparty never received confirmations for several months of deals and had to chase them.
The sender of an executed confirm did not know the route by which confirmation details reach the downstream team.

automation.approach: Generate confirmations from the deal record when a deal is entered, send them to the counterparty and a fixed internal distribution automatically, and track which deals still lack a confirmation so gaps are caught before the counterparty asks.
automation.rationale: The problems shown are about routing: who gets the confirm and whether it was ever sent. A short written procedure naming the distribution and the check for unconfirmed deals addresses both right away.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work is pulling the deal terms, preparing or locating the confirmation and getting it executed or faxed. Around 10 minutes per round; resending several months of missing confirms runs longer. Generating and distributing confirms from the deal record could take most of it, leaving review of terms.

processes.description: ISO and FERC notices on market rules, price caps, settlement figures, operating procedures, outages and calls arrive from CAISO communications and regulatory staff. Bill Williams and others forward the relevant ones to traders and analysts with commentary, ask colleagues what an order means for the desk, set up meetings to discuss pros and cons, request test access for system changes, and review draft documents for comment by stated deadlines.
steps: An ISO, FERC or market notice arrives from CAISO or regulatory staff.
A desk lead reads it and judges whether it affects trading or scheduling.
Relevant notices are forwarded to the team with a summary or question.
The team discusses the impact, sometimes in a meeting, and asks follow-up questions of the ISO.
Comments on drafts are sent back by the stated deadline, and system changes are tested.

stalls.summary: Published market simulation documents had problems in their PDF versions, requiring the material to be reissued.
Notices are repeatedly corrected or revised, such as a correction to a market notice about a FERC order and a later FAQ, so the same order is reviewed more than once.

automation.approach: Route ISO and FERC notices into a single feed tagged by topic (price caps, settlements, operating procedures, outages, calls), and produce a short daily digest that flags notices touching active positions or systems, with a standard impact note format for the desk lead to complete.
automation.rationale: The work is triage of a high volume of notices, many routine. A checklist for assessing a notice's impact (pricing, scheduling, settlements, systems, comment deadline) makes the review consistent while the digest cuts the sorting; the judgement on market impact stays with people.

work_estimate.rationale: Beyond reading, a round involves working out what an order or calculation change means for the desk, discussing it, preparing questions for the ISO, testing system changes, or reviewing a draft for comment. Routine automated notices need little; orders and rule changes need analysis or a meeting, so around 25 minutes with a wide range. Sorting and summarising could be tooled, the impact judgement much less.
